**Main Street Station** is a hotel and casino in downtown Las Vegas, Nevada. It is owned by Boyd Gaming. It originally opened in 1978 as the **Holiday International**, part of the Holiday Inn franchise. The casino portion closed in 1980, due to financial problems, and the hotel closed four years later. The property was renovated by Japanese investor Katsuki Manabe as the **Park Hotel and Casino**, which operated from 1987 to 1990.
Florida developer Bob Snow purchased the property and renovated it further, reopening it as Main Street Station on August 30, 1991. It featured a Victorian theme and various antiques, which came from Snow's personal collection. Snow did not have experience in the gaming industry, and Main Street Station filed for bankruptcy four months after its opening. It closed in June 1992, and was sold to Boyd the following year. The company sometimes used the hotel to house overflow guests from its other downtown properties.

Main Street Station was fully reopened on November 22, 1996, after a $45 million renovation, which included the addition of a microbrewery known as Triple 7. The property's Victorian theme was retained. Main Street Station has 406 rooms and a 26,918 sq ft (2,500.8 m 2) casino. The antique collection includes railroad cars and a portion of the Berlin Wall.
The property began as the Holiday International,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-2) with construction starting in 1976.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-3) The hotel opened in February 1978,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-Riddle-4) with 416 rooms.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-5) The 16-story hotel was part of the Holiday Inn franchise, joining two other area locations, both on the Las Vegas Strip.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-6) The property's casino was opened on June 30, 1978, and was operated by Major Riddle,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-Riddle-4) who leased it from Holiday International owner Louis Walter.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-7)
Sign for the Holiday International, early 1980s

The casino closed in September 1980, after going into bankruptcy.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-lvs1996-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-9) Kenilworth Systems Corporation, based in New York, planned to reopen the casino in 1982 as a testing ground for its cashless, computerized gambling system.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-12) However, Kenilworth soon encountered financial difficulties,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-14) and canceled its plans at the end of the year.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-15) The hotel closed in 1984, following an extended worker strike which affected numerous Las Vegas resorts.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-macy-17)

The property reopened on September 3, 1987,[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-18) as the Park Hotel and Casino. It was developed by Japanese investor Katsuki Manabe,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-lvs1996-8)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-macy-17) who spent approximately $13 million on refurbishments.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-19) Walter remained as owner, leasing the hotel-casino to Manabe.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-complete-20) The property included 435 rooms,[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-21) and 600 employees.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-22)

**Main Street Station** is a hotel and casino in downtown Las Vegas, Nevada. It is owned by Boyd Gaming. It originally opened in 1978 as the **Holiday International**, part of the Holiday Inn franchise. The casino portion closed in 1980, due to financial problems, and the hotel closed four years later. The property was renovated by Japanese investor Katsuki Manabe as the **Park Hotel and Casino**, which operated from 1987 to 1990.
Florida developer Bob Snow purchased the property and renovated it further, reopening it as Main Street Station on August 30, 1991. It featured a Victorian theme and various antiques, which came from Snow's personal collection. Snow did not have experience in the gaming industry, and Main Street Station filed for bankruptcy four months after its opening. It closed in June 1992, and was sold to Boyd the following year. The company sometimes used the hotel to house overflow guests from its other downtown properties.
texts.1:
Main Street Station was fully reopened on November 22, 1996, after a $45 million renovation, which included the addition of a microbrewery known as Triple 7. The property's Victorian theme was retained. Main Street Station has 406 rooms and a 26,918 sq ft (2,500.8 m 2) casino. The antique collection includes railroad cars and a portion of the Berlin Wall.
The property began as the Holiday International,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-2) with construction starting in 1976.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-3) The hotel opened in February 1978,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-Riddle-4) with 416 rooms.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-5) The 16-story hotel was part of the Holiday Inn franchise, joining two other area locations, both on the Las Vegas Strip.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-6) The property's casino was opened on June 30, 1978, and was operated by Major Riddle,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-Riddle-4) who leased it from Holiday International owner Louis Walter.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-7)

texts.2: The casino closed in September 1980, after going into bankruptcy.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-lvs1996-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-9) Kenilworth Systems Corporation, based in New York, planned to reopen the casino in 1982 as a testing ground for its cashless, computerized gambling system.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-12) However, Kenilworth soon encountered financial difficulties,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-14) and canceled its plans at the end of the year.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-15) The hotel closed in 1984, following an extended worker strike which affected numerous Las Vegas resorts.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-macy-17)
texts.3: The property reopened on September 3, 1987,[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-18) as the Park Hotel and Casino. It was developed by Japanese investor Katsuki Manabe,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-lvs1996-8)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-macy-17) who spent approximately $13 million on refurbishments.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-19) Walter remained as owner, leasing the hotel-casino to Manabe.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-complete-20) The property included 435 rooms,[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-21) and 600 employees.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-22)

**Main Street Station** is a hotel and casino in downtown Las Vegas, Nevada. It is owned by Boyd Gaming. It originally opened in 1978 as the **Holiday International**, part of the Holiday Inn franchise. The casino portion closed in 1980, due to financial problems, and the hotel closed four years later. The property was renovated by Japanese investor Katsuki Manabe as the **Park Hotel and Casino**, which operated from 1987 to 1990.
Florida developer Bob Snow purchased the property and renovated it further, reopening it as Main Street Station on August 30, 1991. It featured a Victorian theme and various antiques, which came from Snow's personal collection. Snow did not have experience in the gaming industry, and Main Street Station filed for bankruptcy four months after its opening. It closed in June 1992, and was sold to Boyd the following year. The company sometimes used the hotel to house overflow guests from its other downtown properties.

Main Street Station was fully reopened on November 22, 1996, after a $45 million renovation, which included the addition of a microbrewery known as Triple 7. The property's Victorian theme was retained. Main Street Station has 406 rooms and a 26,918 sq ft (2,500.8 m 2) casino. The antique collection includes railroad cars and a portion of the Berlin Wall.
The property began as the Holiday International,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-2) with construction starting in 1976.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-3) The hotel opened in February 1978,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-Riddle-4) with 416 rooms.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-5) The 16-story hotel was part of the Holiday Inn franchise, joining two other area locations, both on the Las Vegas Strip.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-6) The property's casino was opened on June 30, 1978, and was operated by Major Riddle,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-Riddle-4) who leased it from Holiday International owner Louis Walter.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-7)
Sign for the Holiday International, early 1980s

The casino closed in September 1980, after going into bankruptcy.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-lvs1996-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-9) Kenilworth Systems Corporation, based in New York, planned to reopen the casino in 1982 as a testing ground for its cashless, computerized gambling system.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-12) However, Kenilworth soon encountered financial difficulties,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-14) and canceled its plans at the end of the year.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-15) The hotel closed in 1984, following an extended worker strike which affected numerous Las Vegas resorts.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-macy-17)

The property reopened on September 3, 1987,[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-18) as the Park Hotel and Casino. It was developed by Japanese investor Katsuki Manabe,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-lvs1996-8)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-macy-17) who spent approximately $13 million on refurbishments.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-19) Walter remained as owner, leasing the hotel-casino to Manabe.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-complete-20) The property included 435 rooms,[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-21) and 600 employees.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street_Station_(hotel_and_casino)#cite_note-22)

Location of Challenger Deep within the Mariana Trench and western Pacific Ocean
The **Challenger Deep** is the deepest known point of the seabed of Earth, located in the western Pacific Ocean at the southern end of the Mariana Trench, in the ocean territory of the Federated States of Micronesia.

The GEBCO Gazetteer of Undersea Feature Names indicates that the feature is situated at 11°22.4′N 142°35.5′E / 11.3733°N 142.5917°E and has an approximated maximum depth of 5,962 to 6,020 fathoms (10,903 to 11,009 m; 35,772 to 36,120 ft)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Deep#cite_note-20210419TOS-1) below sea level. A 2011 study placed the depth at 5,971±5 fathoms (10,920±9 m; 35,826±30 ft)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Deep#cite_note-GEBCO_Gazetteer_of_Undersea_Feature_Names-2) with a 2021 study revising the value to 10,935±6 m (35,876±20 ft) at a 95% confidence level.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Deep#cite_note-20211021ORP-3)
The depression is named after the British Royal Navy survey ships HMS _Challenger_, whose expedition of 1872–1876 first located it, and HMS _Challenger II_, whose expedition of 1950–1952 established its record-setting depth.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Deep#cite_note-:1-4) The first descent by any vehicle was conducted by the United States Navy using the bathyscaphe_Trieste_ in January 1960. As of July 2022, there were 27 people who have descended to the Challenger Deep.
Sonar mapping of the Challenger Deep by the DSSV _Pressure Drop_ employing a Kongsberg SIMRAD EM124 multibeam echosounder system (26 April – 4 May 2019)

The Challenger Deep is a relatively small slot-shaped depression in the bottom of a considerably larger crescent-shaped oceanic trench, which itself is an unusually deep feature in the ocean floor. The Challenger Deep consists of three basins, each six to ten kilometres (3.7 to 6.2mi) long, 2 kilometres (1.2 mi) wide, and over 5,930 fathoms (10,840 m; 35,580 ft) in depth, oriented in echelon from west to east, separated by mounds between the basins 200 to 300 metres (660 to 980 ft) higher. The three basins feature extends about 48 kilometres (30 mi) west to east if measured at the 10,650-metre (34,940 ft)isobath.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Deep#cite_note-5) Both the western and eastern basins have recorded depths (by sonar bathymetry) in excess of 10,920 metres (35,827 ft), while the center basin is slightly less deep.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Deep#cite_note-Stewart,_Heather_&_Jamieson,_Alan._(2019)-6) The closest land to the Challenger Deep is Fais Island (one of the outer islands of Yap), 155 nautical miles (287 km; 178 mi) southwest, and Guam, 164 nautical miles (304 km; 189 mi) to the northeast.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Deep#cite_note-7) Detailed sonar mapping of the western, center and eastern basins in June 2020 by the DSSV _Pressure Drop_ combined with manned descents revealed that they undulate with slopes and piles of rocks above a bed of pelagic ooze. This conforms with the description of Challenger Deep as consisting of an elongated seabed section with distinct sub-basins or sediment-filled pools.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Deep#cite_note-20211021ORP-3)

The topography above is explained by the complex subduction of tectonic plates.
The summary report of the HMS _Challenger_ expedition lists unicellular life forms from two dredged samples, taken when the Challenger Deep was first discovered.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Deep#cite_note-8) These (_Nassellaria_ and _Spumellaria_) were reported in the Report on Radiolaria (1887)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Deep#cite_note-9) written by Ernst Haeckel.
On their 1960 descent, the crew of the _Trieste_ noted that the floor consisted of diatomaceous ooze and reported observing "some type of flatfish" lying on the seabed.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Deep#cite_note-10)
> And as we were settling this final fathom, I saw a wonderful thing. Lying on the bottom just beneath us was some type of flatfish, resembling a sole, about 1 foot [30 cm] long and 6 inches [15 cm] across. Even as I saw him, his two round eyes on top of his head spied us–a monster of steel–invading his silent realm. Eyes? Why should he have eyes? Merely to see phosphorescence? The floodlight that bathed him was the first real light ever to enter this hadal realm. Here, in an instant, was the answer that biologists had asked for the decades. Could life exist in the greatest depths of the ocean? It could! And not only that, here apparently, was a true, bony teleost fish, not a primitive ray or elasmobranch. Location of the Mariana Trench
The **Mariana Trench** is the deepest oceanic trench on Earth, located in the western Pacific Ocean, about 200 kilometers (124 mi) east of the Mariana Islands. It is crescent-shaped and measures about 2,550 km (1,580 mi) in length and 69 km (43 mi) in width. The maximum known depth is 10,935±6 meters (35,876±20 ft; 5,979.3±3.3 fathoms; 6.7947±0.0037 mi) at the southern end of a small slot-shaped valley in its floor known as the Challenger Deep.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench#cite_note-:5-1) This makes the deepest point of the trench more than 2 km (1.2 mi) farther from sea level than the peak of Mount Everest.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench#cite_note-3)

At the bottom of the trench the water column above exerts a pressure of 111 MPa (16,100 psi), approximately 1,100 times the standard atmospheric pressure at sea level or eight tons per square inch.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench#cite_note-4)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench#cite_note-5) The temperature at the bottom is 1 to 4°C (34 to 39°F).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench#cite_note-6)
In 2009, the United States established the Mariana Trench Marine National Monument as national monument from the parts of the Mariana Trench that are inside the exclusive economic zone (EEZ) of the United States.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench#cite_note-7) This does not include the Challenger Deep, which lies inside the EEZ of the Federated States of Micronesia.
Single-celled organisms called monothalamea have been found in the trench at a record depth of 10.6 km (35,000 ft; 6.6 mi) below the sea surface by researchers from the Scripps Institution of Oceanography.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench#cite_note-gaf-8) Data has also suggested that microbial life forms thrive within the trench.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench#cite_note-LS-20130317-9)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench#cite_note-NG-20130317-10)

## Etymology
The Mariana Trench is named after the nearby Mariana Islands,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench#cite_note-11) which are named Las Marianas in honor of Spanish Queen Mariana of Austria.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench#cite_note-12) The islands are part of the island arc that is formed on an over-riding plate, called the Mariana plate (also named for the islands), on the western side of the trench.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench#cite_note-:0-13)

## Geology
The Pacific plate is subducted beneath the Mariana plate, creating the Mariana trench, and (further on) the arc of the Mariana Islands, as water trapped in the plate is released and explodes upward to form island volcanoes and earthquakes.
The Mariana Trench is part of the Izu–Bonin–Marianasubduction system that forms the boundary between two tectonic plates. In this system, the western edge of one plate, the Pacific plate, is subducted (i.e., thrust) beneath the smaller Mariana plate that lies to the west. Crustal material at the western edge of the Pacific plate is some of the oldest oceanic crust on Earth (up to 170 million years old), and is cooler and denser; hence its great height difference relative to the higher-riding (and younger) Mariana plate. The deepest area at the plate boundary is the Mariana Trench proper.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench#cite_note-14)
The movement of the Pacific and Mariana plates is also indirectly responsible for the formation of the Mariana Islands. These volcanic islands are caused by flux melting of the upper mantle due to the release of water that is trapped in minerals of the subducted portion of the Pacific plate.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench#cite_note-15)

## Research history
Ocean trenches in the western Pacific
The trench was first discovered during routine depth sounding of the region during the _Challenger_ expedition in 1875 using a weighted rope, which recorded a depth of 4,475 fathoms (8,184 meters; 26,850 feet).[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench#cite_note-:0-13)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench#cite_note-16) In 1877, a map was published called _Tiefenkarte des Grossen Ozeans_ ("Depth map of the Great Ocean") by Petermann, which showed a _Challenger Tief_ ("Challenger deep") at the location of that sounding. In 1899, USS _Nero_, a converted collier, recorded a depth of 5,269 fathoms (9,636 meters; 31,614 feet).[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench#cite_note-Theberge-17)
In 1951, under Chief Scientist Thomas Gaskell, _Challenger II_ surveyed the trench using echo sounding, a much more precise and vastly easier way to measure depth than the sounding equipment and drag lines used in the original expedition. During this survey, the deepest part of the trench was recorded when the _Challenger II_ measured a depth of 5,960 fathoms (10,900 meters; 35,760 feet) at 11°19′N 142°15′E / 11.317°N 142.250°E,[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench#cite_note-18) known as the Challenger Deep.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench#cite_note-marianatrench.com-19)

Located east of the Philippines, the Mariana Trench is also massive. It is 120 times larger than the Grand Canyon and includes millions of acres virtually unknown to humans. In January of 2009, the Marianas Trench Marine National Monument was established. On the same date, Jan. 16, 2009, the Mariana Trench and Mariana Arc of Fire national wildlife refuges were also established. Some species exclusively survive on bacteria from hydrothermal vents that spill out highly acidic, boiling water. In other areas of the marine monument, one coral reef has the highest density of sharks anywhere in the Pacific Ocean, while another has one of the most diverse collections of stony coral. This amazing video footage was captured in 2016 by a rover launched from the NOAA ship Okeanos Explorer. The rover was only able to reach about halfway down into the Mariana Trench. Location of Challenger Deep within the Mariana Trench and western Pacific Ocean
The **Challenger Deep** is the deepest known point of the seabed of Earth, located in the western Pacific Ocean at the southern end of the Mariana Trench, in the ocean territory of the Federated States of Micronesia.
texts.1:
The GEBCO Gazetteer of Undersea Feature Names indicates that the feature is situated at 11°22.4′N 142°35.5′E / 11.3733°N 142.5917°E and has an approximated maximum depth of 5,962 to 6,020 fathoms (10,903 to 11,009 m; 35,772 to 36,120 ft)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Deep#cite_note-20210419TOS-1) below sea level. A 2011 study placed the depth at 5,971±5 fathoms (10,920±9 m; 35,826±30 ft)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Deep#cite_note-GEBCO_Gazetteer_of_Undersea_Feature_Names-2) with a 2021 study revising the value to 10,935±6 m (35,876±20 ft) at a 95% confidence level.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Deep#cite_note-20211021ORP-3)
The depression is named after the British Royal Navy survey ships HMS _Challenger_, whose expedition of 1872–1876 first located it, and HMS _Challenger II_, whose expedition of 1950–1952 established its record-setting depth.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Deep#cite_note-:1-4) The first descent by any vehicle was conducted by the United States Navy using the bathyscaphe_Trieste_ in January 1960. As of July 2022, there were 27 people who have descended to the Challenger Deep.
Sonar mapping of the Challenger Deep by the DSSV _Pressure Drop_ employing a Kongsberg SIMRAD EM124 multibeam echosounder system (26 April – 4 May 2019)
texts.2: The Challenger Deep is a relatively small slot-shaped depression in the bottom of a considerably larger crescent-shaped oceanic trench, which itself is an unusually deep feature in the ocean floor. The Challenger Deep consists of three basins, each six to ten kilometres (3.7 to 6.2mi) long, 2 kilometres (1.2 mi) wide, and over 5,930 fathoms (10,840 m; 35,580 ft) in depth, oriented in echelon from west to east, separated by mounds between the basins 200 to 300 metres (660 to 980 ft) higher. The three basins feature extends about 48 kilometres (30 mi) west to east if measured at the 10,650-metre (34,940 ft)isobath.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Deep#cite_note-5) Both the western and eastern basins have recorded depths (by sonar bathymetry) in excess of 10,920 metres (35,827 ft), while the center basin is slightly less deep.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Deep#cite_note-Stewart,_Heather_&_Jamieson,_Alan._(2019)-6) The closest land to the Challenger Deep is Fais Island (one of the outer islands of Yap), 155 nautical miles (287 km; 178 mi) southwest, and Guam, 164 nautical miles (304 km; 189 mi) to the northeast.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Deep#cite_note-7) Detailed sonar mapping of the western, center and eastern basins in June 2020 by the DSSV _Pressure Drop_ combined with manned descents revealed that they undulate with slopes and piles of rocks above a bed of pelagic ooze. This conforms with the description of Challenger Deep as consisting of an elongated seabed section with distinct sub-basins or sediment-filled pools.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Deep#cite_note-20211021ORP-3)
texts.3:
The topography above is explained by the complex subduction of tectonic plates.
The summary report of the HMS _Challenger_ expedition lists unicellular life forms from two dredged samples, taken when the Challenger Deep was first discovered.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Deep#cite_note-8) These (_Nassellaria_ and _Spumellaria_) were reported in the Report on Radiolaria (1887)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Deep#cite_note-9) written by Ernst Haeckel.
On their 1960 descent, the crew of the _Trieste_ noted that the floor consisted of diatomaceous ooze and reported observing "some type of flatfish" lying on the seabed.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Deep#cite_note-10)
> And as we were settling this final fathom, I saw a wonderful thing. Lying on the bottom just beneath us was some type of flatfish, resembling a sole, about 1 foot [30 cm] long and 6 inches [15 cm] across. Even as I saw him, his two round eyes on top of his head spied us–a monster of steel–invading his silent realm. Eyes? Why should he have eyes? Merely to see phosphorescence? The floodlight that bathed him was the first real light ever to enter this hadal realm. Here, in an instant, was the answer that biologists had asked for the decades. Could life exist in the greatest depths of the ocean? It could! And not only that, here apparently, was a true, bony teleost fish, not a primitive ray or elasmobranch. Yes, a highly evolved vertebrate, in time's arrow very close to man himself. Slowly, extremely slowly, this flatfish swam away. Moving along the bottom, partly in the ooze and partly in the water, he disappeared into his night. Slowly too–perhaps everything is slow at the bottom of the sea–Walsh and I shook hands.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Deep#cite_note-11)

Location of the Mariana Trench
The **Mariana Trench** is the deepest oceanic trench on Earth, located in the western Pacific Ocean, about 200 kilometers (124 mi) east of the Mariana Islands. It is crescent-shaped and measures about 2,550 km (1,580 mi) in length and 69 km (43 mi) in width. The maximum known depth is 10,935±6 meters (35,876±20 ft; 5,979.3±3.3 fathoms; 6.7947±0.0037 mi) at the southern end of a small slot-shaped valley in its floor known as the Challenger Deep.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench#cite_note-:5-1) This makes the deepest point of the trench more than 2 km (1.2 mi) farther from sea level than the peak of Mount Everest.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench#cite_note-3)

At the bottom of the trench the water column above exerts a pressure of 111 MPa (16,100 psi), approximately 1,100 times the standard atmospheric pressure at sea level or eight tons per square inch.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench#cite_note-4)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench#cite_note-5) The temperature at the bottom is 1 to 4°C (34 to 39°F).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench#cite_note-6)
In 2009, the United States established the Mariana Trench Marine National Monument as national monument from the parts of the Mariana Trench that are inside the exclusive economic zone (EEZ) of the United States.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench#cite_note-7) This does not include the Challenger Deep, which lies inside the EEZ of the Federated States of Micronesia.
Single-celled organisms called monothalamea have been found in the trench at a record depth of 10.6 km (35,000 ft; 6.6 mi) below the sea surface by researchers from the Scripps Institution of Oceanography.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench#cite_note-gaf-8) Data has also suggested that microbial life forms thrive within the trench.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench#cite_note-LS-20130317-9)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench#cite_note-NG-20130317-10)

## Etymology
The Mariana Trench is named after the nearby Mariana Islands,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench#cite_note-11) which are named Las Marianas in honor of Spanish Queen Mariana of Austria.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench#cite_note-12) The islands are part of the island arc that is formed on an over-riding plate, called the Mariana plate (also named for the islands), on the western side of the trench.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench#cite_note-:0-13)

## Geology
The Pacific plate is subducted beneath the Mariana plate, creating the Mariana trench, and (further on) the arc of the Mariana Islands, as water trapped in the plate is released and explodes upward to form island volcanoes and earthquakes.
The Mariana Trench is part of the Izu–Bonin–Marianasubduction system that forms the boundary between two tectonic plates. In this system, the western edge of one plate, the Pacific plate, is subducted (i.e., thrust) beneath the smaller Mariana plate that lies to the west. Crustal material at the western edge of the Pacific plate is some of the oldest oceanic crust on Earth (up to 170 million years old), and is cooler and denser; hence its great height difference relative to the higher-riding (and younger) Mariana plate. The deepest area at the plate boundary is the Mariana Trench proper.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench#cite_note-14)
The movement of the Pacific and Mariana plates is also indirectly responsible for the formation of the Mariana Islands. These volcanic islands are caused by flux melting of the upper mantle due to the release of water that is trapped in minerals of the subducted portion of the Pacific plate.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench#cite_note-15)

## Research history
Ocean trenches in the western Pacific
The trench was first discovered during routine depth sounding of the region during the _Challenger_ expedition in 1875 using a weighted rope, which recorded a depth of 4,475 fathoms (8,184 meters; 26,850 feet).[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench#cite_note-:0-13)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench#cite_note-16) In 1877, a map was published called _Tiefenkarte des Grossen Ozeans_ ("Depth map of the Great Ocean") by Petermann, which showed a _Challenger Tief_ ("Challenger deep") at the location of that sounding. In 1899, USS _Nero_, a converted collier, recorded a depth of 5,269 fathoms (9,636 meters; 31,614 feet).[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench#cite_note-Theberge-17)
In 1951, under Chief Scientist Thomas Gaskell, _Challenger II_ surveyed the trench using echo sounding, a much more precise and vastly easier way to measure depth than the sounding equipment and drag lines used in the original expedition. During this survey, the deepest part of the trench was recorded when the _Challenger II_ measured a depth of 5,960 fathoms (10,900 meters; 35,760 feet) at 11°19′N 142°15′E / 11.317°N 142.250°E,[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench#cite_note-18) known as the Challenger Deep.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench#cite_note-marianatrench.com-19)

This underwater world includes mud volcanoes, one of which “produces almost pure liquid carbon dioxide,” according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), and another that has a pool of liquid sulfur. Some species exclusively survive on bacteria from hydrothermal vents that spill out highly acidic, boiling water. In other areas of the marine monument, one coral reef has the highest density of sharks anywhere in the Pacific Ocean, while another has one of the most diverse collections of stony coral. This amazing video footage was captured in 2016 by a rover launched from the NOAA ship Okeanos Explorer. The rover was only able to reach about halfway down into the Mariana Trench. Location of Challenger Deep within the Mariana Trench and western Pacific Ocean
The **Challenger Deep** is the deepest known point of the seabed of Earth, located in the western Pacific Ocean at the southern end of the Mariana Trench, in the ocean territory of the Federated States of Micronesia.

The GEBCO Gazetteer of Undersea Feature Names indicates that the feature is situated at 11°22.4′N 142°35.5′E / 11.3733°N 142.5917°E and has an approximated maximum depth of 5,962 to 6,020 fathoms (10,903 to 11,009 m; 35,772 to 36,120 ft)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Deep#cite_note-20210419TOS-1) below sea level. A 2011 study placed the depth at 5,971±5 fathoms (10,920±9 m; 35,826±30 ft)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Deep#cite_note-GEBCO_Gazetteer_of_Undersea_Feature_Names-2) with a 2021 study revising the value to 10,935±6 m (35,876±20 ft) at a 95% confidence level.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Deep#cite_note-20211021ORP-3)
The depression is named after the British Royal Navy survey ships HMS _Challenger_, whose expedition of 1872–1876 first located it, and HMS _Challenger II_, whose expedition of 1950–1952 established its record-setting depth.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Deep#cite_note-:1-4) The first descent by any vehicle was conducted by the United States Navy using the bathyscaphe_Trieste_ in January 1960. As of July 2022, there were 27 people who have descended to the Challenger Deep.
Sonar mapping of the Challenger Deep by the DSSV _Pressure Drop_ employing a Kongsberg SIMRAD EM124 multibeam echosounder system (26 April – 4 May 2019)

The Challenger Deep is a relatively small slot-shaped depression in the bottom of a considerably larger crescent-shaped oceanic trench, which itself is an unusually deep feature in the ocean floor. The Challenger Deep consists of three basins, each six to ten kilometres (3.7 to 6.2mi) long, 2 kilometres (1.2 mi) wide, and over 5,930 fathoms (10,840 m; 35,580 ft) in depth, oriented in echelon from west to east, separated by mounds between the basins 200 to 300 metres (660 to 980 ft) higher. The three basins feature extends about 48 kilometres (30 mi) west to east if measured at the 10,650-metre (34,940 ft)isobath.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Deep#cite_note-5) Both the western and eastern basins have recorded depths (by sonar bathymetry) in excess of 10,920 metres (35,827 ft), while the center basin is slightly less deep.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Deep#cite_note-Stewart,_Heather_&_Jamieson,_Alan._(2019)-6) The closest land to the Challenger Deep is Fais Island (one of the outer islands of Yap), 155 nautical miles (287 km; 178 mi) southwest, and Guam, 164 nautical miles (304 km; 189 mi) to the northeast.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Deep#cite_note-7) Detailed sonar mapping of the western, center and eastern basins in June 2020 by the DSSV _Pressure Drop_ combined with manned descents revealed that they undulate with slopes and piles of rocks above a bed of pelagic ooze. This conforms with the description of Challenger Deep as consisting of an elongated seabed section with distinct sub-basins or sediment-filled pools.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Deep#cite_note-20211021ORP-3)

The topography above is explained by the complex subduction of tectonic plates.
The summary report of the HMS _Challenger_ expedition lists unicellular life forms from two dredged samples, taken when the Challenger Deep was first discovered.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Deep#cite_note-8) These (_Nassellaria_ and _Spumellaria_) were reported in the Report on Radiolaria (1887)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Deep#cite_note-9) written by Ernst Haeckel.
On their 1960 descent, the crew of the _Trieste_ noted that the floor consisted of diatomaceous ooze and reported observing "some type of flatfish" lying on the seabed.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Deep#cite_note-10)
> And as we were settling this final fathom, I saw a wonderful thing. Lying on the bottom just beneath us was some type of flatfish, resembling a sole, about 1 foot [30 cm] long and 6 inches [15 cm] across. Even as I saw him, his two round eyes on top of his head spied us–a monster of steel–invading his silent realm. Eyes? Why should he have eyes? Merely to see phosphorescence? The floodlight that bathed him was the first real light ever to enter this hadal realm. Here, in an instant, was the answer that biologists had asked for the decades. Could life exist in the greatest depths of the ocean? It could! And not only that, here apparently, was a true, bony teleost fish, not a primitive ray or elasmobranch. Yes, a highly evolved vertebrate, in time's arrow very close to man himself. Slowly, extremely slowly, this flatfish swam away. Moving along the bottom, partly in the ooze and partly in the water, he disappeared into his night. Slowly too–perhaps everything is slow at the bottom of the sea–Walsh and I shook hands.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Deep#cite_note-11)
